```{r, include = FALSE}
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4

```

With the default options, `spei()` and `spi()` compute the indices as they
were originally defined. This vignette explains the options that change how
they are computed, and when it makes sense to use them:

- the time scale and the kernel;
- the probability distribution and the fitting method;
- the reference period, and reusing fitted parameters;
- missing values, and values outside the fitted distribution.

We use the `wichita` data, as in `vignette("SPEI")`:

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)

data(wichita)
wichita <- ts(wichita[, -c(1, 2)], start = c(1980, 1), frequency = 12)
prcp <- wichita[, "PRCP"]
bal <- prcp - hargreaves(wichita[, "TMIN"], wichita[, "TMAX"],
  lat = 37.6475, verbose = FALSE
)
```

Setting `verbose = FALSE` silences the report of the options used, which
the functions print by default.

## Time scale

The time scale, `scale`, is the number of months over which the data are
accumulated before standardizing. It sets the memory of the index:

- 1 to 3 months: conditions of the soil surface, rain-fed crops in the
  growing season, flows in small catchments;
- 6 to 12 months: river flows, reservoir storage;
- 12 to 48 months: groundwater and other slow systems.

These ranges are only indicative. The time scale that best matches a given
system is usually found by computing the index at many scales and
correlating each with an observed variable, such as crop yields or tree-ring
widths.

## Kernel

By default, all the months in the time scale have the same weight (a
rectangular kernel). The `kernel` argument gives more weight to the recent
months, with the shapes `"triangular"`, `"circular"` and `"gaussian"`:

```{r, fig.alt = "Weights of the rectangular, triangular, circular and gaussian kernels over 12 months"}
k <- sapply(c("rectangular", "triangular", "circular", "gaussian"),
  function(type) kern(12, type)
)
matplot(0:11, k, type = "l", lty = 1, col = 1:4,
  xlab = "Months before the current one", ylab = "Weight"
)
legend("topright", colnames(k), col = 1:4, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

`shift` moves the highest weight back in time, by a number of months.
See `?kern` for details.

```{r}
spei12 <- spei(bal, 12, verbose = FALSE)
spei12_gau <- spei(bal, 12,
  kernel = list(type = "gaussian", shift = 0), verbose = FALSE
)
cor(spei12$fitted, spei12_gau$fitted, use = "complete.obs")
```

The rectangular kernel is the standard definition, and the one to use for
results that should be comparable with other studies.

## Distribution

For each calendar month, the functions fit a probability distribution to the
accumulated values, and convert each value to the standard normal scale
through its cumulative probability. Three distributions are available:

| Distribution | Default for | Data |
|---|---|---|
| `"log-Logistic"` | `spei()` | any values, including negative ones |
| `"Gamma"` | `spi()` | non-negative values only |
| `"PearsonIII"` | | non-negative values only |

**For the SPEI, use the log-Logistic distribution.** The water balance can be
negative, and the three-parameter log-Logistic fits it well across climates.
The Gamma and PearsonIII distributions are fitted to positive values only;
negative values get a warning and the lowest possible index value.

**For the SPI, the Gamma distribution is the standard**, as defined by
McKee et al. (1993). The PearsonIII distribution has a third parameter, for
the shape, so it is more flexible and can fit skewed precipitation better;
Guttman (1999) recommended it for the SPI, and it can be preferred, at the
cost of departing from the original definition.
Months with zero
precipitation are handled through the probability of zero precipitation
(`pze`) in each calendar month: the fitted distribution covers only the
positive values, and the zeros get an index value set by `pze`, the share
of zeros in that calendar month. Wichita has four months with no precipitation; this is
how each distribution handles them at a 1-month scale:

```{r}
spi1 <- sapply(c("Gamma", "PearsonIII", "log-Logistic"),
  function(d) spi(prcp, 1, distribution = d, verbose = FALSE)$fitted
)
round(spi1[prcp == 0, ], 2)
```

The distributions can also differ in the tails. With positive skew, as is usual
for precipitation, the PearsonIII distribution is bounded below, and here it
returns `-Inf`
for three months whose precipitation falls below that bound:

```{r}
colSums(is.infinite(spi1))
```

See the section [Values outside the fitted distribution](#values-outside-the-fitted-distribution)
below.

## Fitting method

The parameters of the distribution are estimated, by default, with unbiased
probability-weighted moments (`fit = "ub-pwm"`). Two alternatives are
available:

- `"pp-pwm"`: probability-weighted moments based on plotting positions;
- `"max-lik"`: maximum likelihood, for the log-Logistic distribution only.
  It starts from the `ub-pwm` estimates. For Gamma and PearsonIII it gives a
  warning and uses `ub-pwm`.

```{r, fig.alt = "SPEI-3 computed with the pp-pwm and max-lik fits plotted against the default ub-pwm fit"}
fits <- sapply(c("ub-pwm", "pp-pwm", "max-lik"),
  function(f) spei(bal, 3, fit = f, verbose = FALSE)$fitted
)
plot(fits[, "ub-pwm"], fits[, "pp-pwm"], col = 2,
  xlab = "SPEI-3, ub-pwm", ylab = "SPEI-3, other fits"
)
points(fits[, "ub-pwm"], fits[, "max-lik"], col = 4)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("pp-pwm", "max-lik"), col = c(2, 4), pch = 1, bty = "n")
```

The three methods agree closely near the centre of the distribution, and
differ more in the tails, where the values depend on the shape of the
fitted distribution. With about 30 values per calendar month, as here,
`ub-pwm` is robust and is the method used in the original definition and in
the SPEIbase dataset. Maximum likelihood can be more efficient with long
series, but it is slower.

## Reference period

By default, the distributions are fitted to the whole series. With
`ref.start` and `ref.end`, they are fitted to a reference period only, and
the index is then computed for the whole series relative to that period.
This requires `data` to be a time series, with the dates given as
year and month:

```{r}
spei12_ref <- spei(bal, 12,
  ref.start = c(1980, 1), ref.end = c(1999, 12), verbose = FALSE
)
round(window(cbind(all = spei12$fitted, ref = spei12_ref$fitted),
  start = c(2011, 6)
), 2)
```

A fixed reference period, such as 1981–2010 or 1991–2020, makes the values
comparable between studies and over time, because adding new data doesn't
change the past values. It is also the way to measure change relative to a
baseline: with a reference period early in the record, a trend towards
drier conditions shows as an increasing frequency of negative values.

Values outside the reference period can lie beyond the range of the
distribution fitted to it. See the last section.

## Reusing the fitted parameters

The fitted parameters are stored in the `coefficients` element of the
result, as an array with one set per series and calendar month:

```{r}
spei12_80s90s <- spei(window(bal, end = c(1999, 12)), 12, verbose = FALSE)
dim(spei12_80s90s$coefficients)
dimnames(spei12_80s90s$coefficients)[[1]]
```

Passing them through `params` computes the index of new data with those
parameters, without fitting again. This is how an operational drought
monitor works: the parameters are fitted once to a reference period and
then applied to each new month. The result equals that of the reference
period option:

```{r}
spei12_new <- spei(bal, 12, params = spei12_80s90s$coefficients,
  verbose = FALSE
)
all.equal(spei12_new$fitted, spei12_ref$fitted)
```

`distribution` must be the same as in the call that produced the
parameters. For Gamma and PearsonIII, the array also holds the probability
of zero precipitation, `pze`, of the reference period.

## Missing values

By default, the data must not have missing values. With `na.rm = TRUE`, the
missing values are left out of the fitting, and the index is `NA` where the
accumulated value is missing. At a scale of 12 months, a single missing
month makes 12 values of the index missing:

```{r}
bal_gap <- bal
bal_gap[100] <- NA
spei12_gap <- spei(bal_gap, 12, na.rm = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
sum(is.na(spei12_gap$fitted)) - sum(is.na(spei12$fitted))
```

A calendar month with no data, or with the same value every year, can't be
fitted, and its index is `NA`.

## Values outside the fitted distribution

The log-Logistic and PearsonIII distributions fitted by `ub-pwm` are
bounded on one side. A value beyond the bound has a probability of exactly 0
or 1, and the index is `-Inf` or `Inf`. This happens mostly in two cases:

- with a reference period, for values outside it that are more extreme than
  any value in it;
- in very dry climates, where the distribution of the water balance is
  highly skewed.

```{r}
sum(is.infinite(spei12_ref$fitted))
```

These values are real extremes: they are beyond anything in the data the
distribution was fitted to. How to treat them depends on the use. For maps
and statistics it is common to set them to a large finite value, such as
±3, rather than leaving them out:

```{r}
x <- spei12_ref$fitted
x[x == Inf] <- 3
x[x == -Inf] <- -3
```

If they are frequent, check the reference period and the distribution:
a longer reference period, or a different distribution, may fit the data
better.

calculation algorithm. *Journal of the American Water Resources
Association*, 35(2), 311–322.

McKee, T.B., Doesken, N.J., Kleist, J. (1993). The relationship of drought

Meteorological Society, Boston, 179–184.
